INTRODUCTION

This study has four interrelated goals: to construct a ceramic
chronology, based primarily on recently excavated pottery from Nippur,
for the range of time from the onset of the decline of the Kassite king-
dom until the rise of the Neo-Babylonian empire (c. 1225-625 B.C.); to
revise the published stratigraphy of Levels VIII-II from Area TA at
Nippur; to describe the archaeological remains of Nippur during the late
second and early first millennia B.C.; and, finally, to relate Nippur's
archaeological remains from this span of time to what is known of the
city's historical and environmental setting.

For Babylonia as a whole the period between the collapse of the
Kassite kingdom and the Neo-Babylonian political renaissance was gener—
ally a time of political instability, military impotence, and economic
impoverishment; politically and economically, it represented the nadir
of Babylonian civilization. Only during the last hundred and twenty
years or so of the period were there the sustained economic growth and
stable political power that culminated in the rise of Nabopolassar's
dynasty.

Not only was Babylonia poor, but the history and archaeology of

There are several reasons why this has been the case, despite the
excavation of many of the cities that are known to have been occupied
during all or part of this period. The most important of these stem
from the nature of the period itself. This was not a time of wealth and
power in Babylonia, and few great public works—-palaces or temples——
would have been built by the rulers. Indeed, no buildings can be
assigned to any reign between 1047 and 722 B.C.> In excavations it has
been repeatedly found that important Kassite buildings did not undergo
major renovation or rebuilding until the last century before Neo-
Babylonian rule, at the earliest.© Since the focus of so much archae-
ological attention in the past has been these great public buildings, it
is not surprising that so little attributable to this span of time has
been reported. Moreover, tablets and inscriptions, which in good ar-
chaeological context could be used to help date building levels and
associated pottery, have not been found.

Archaeologists, of course, regularly have to date levels, buil-
dings, pottery, and other artifacts in the absence of textual evidence;
indeed the presence of written texts is the exception rather than the
rule in most situations. But progress in this regard has been slow in

the case of post-Kassite Babylonia chiefly because of the poor methodol-

Building C

Only a fraction of Building C has thus far been recovered; but it
is clear from its plan, construction, and contents that, in Level II at
least, this was no ordinary domestic dwelling (fig. 7). There was a
small room at the southeast end of the building with a broad niche in
the wall opposite the door (Locus 173). The door of this room led out
to a paved courtyard from which a well had been sunk (Locus 195). More-
over, behind Locus 173 was a rank of rooms (Loci 325, 300/329, 311), all
of which opened onto the street. The typical Babylonian house, in con—
trast, presented a blank wall to the street, broken by only a single
door.

Building C was constructed with evident foresight and deliberation.
Its foundation, thus far seen only under Loci 173 and 195, was built in
several steps. The bottom of the foundation was laid on top of the
irregular surface beneath the building (Walls MA and MC in fig. 11).

The space thus enclosed was then filled with gray, ashy soil and mud—
brick rubble. Inexplicably, the top of this fill was not leveled, at
least not under Locus 173; but its surface was mounded up. This

mounded-up fill and the low walls which contained it were then covered

with reeds or reed mats. At this stage, the foundation under Locus 173

covering both the fill and the foundation walls; and the walls of the

curved like the mounded-up fill beneath it, and its edges, particularly
the northwest end, were lower than the middle; so a packing of mudbricks
and baked bricks was apparently used to help level the floor. This
effort was not entirely successful: the northwestern end of the room
was raised, but the floor still tipped down to the sides.

gray, ashy soil with mudbrick inclusions that had been used earlier.

of reddish clay plaster.

Area WC-2; and three buildings have been examined, two houses and a
structure that may have had a more public character. Level II lasted
long enough for approximately one~half meter of earth floors to accumu-
late in several of the rooms of House A. Accumulations were somewhat
thinner in Buildings B and C, but about the same time all three buil-—
dings were abandoned. Building A was left clean; but in parts of
Buildings B and C whole vessels littered the floor, and in the former

provide an approximate terminus post quem of sometime during or after

Ashurbanipal Ekur bricks, one each from Buildings B and C, and a tablet
dated to the reign of Shamash-shuma-ukin found on a living floor in

All three buildings were rebuilt in Level I, at about the same
time. They seem to have kept the same property lines as before, but
their plans were altered significantly. Building A, where several in-

subdivided into two separate units, the smaller to the northwest, the
larger to the southeast. In Building C, the Level II chapel was not
reconstructed; and the plans of other rooms were altered. In all three
buildings, the construction in Level I was inferior to Level II, with
thinner walls made of poorer-quality mud bricks. Shortly after the
initial Level I construction (Level ID), there was a second abandonment,
at least in Buildings A and B. Building A was carefully sealed up be-
fore the departure of the inhabitants; but Building B, as in Level II,
showed signs of a hasty departure, with numerous items, some of them
seemingly valuable, being left behind. Thereafter Building A and the
northwestern rooms of Building B were permanently abandoned. The re—

mainder of Building B and most of Building C continued to be occupied

for some time before they too were abandoned, and the southern end of
Nippur was never again inhabited.

Evidence as to the quality of life in Level I was contradictory.
Architecturally the level represented a decline, with thinner walls than
before and poor-quality mud bricks; in the room arrangements of Building
B, the occupants seemed to be just making do, not reoccupying abandoned
portions of the property. On the other hand, the final pavement in the
Building B courtyard was the best-laid in that building; it was cer-
tainly better than the rough, rubbly pavement of the otherwise more
solidly built Level II house. Moreover, the quality of the small finds
of Level I equalled that of Level II. Level I yielded copper or bronze
vessels, many iron implements, numerous fine-quality pottery vessels,
including glazed bottles that must have contained expensive oils or
perfumes, and clay plaques of genuine artistic merit. Even at the end
of its existence, this was not an impoverished settlement. The wealth
of the residents, as attested by the small finds, was well above subsis—
tence level; yet there was an apparent reluctance to invest in improving
real property in this part of the city. Taken together, the evidence
suggests that, from the end of Level II on, life became increasingly
unsettled at the southern end of the city and at times was even risky.
During this period, a wall was built to protect this area; but the set-

tlement dwindled, a house at a time, until it was entirely abandoned.

of the courtyard. The Level IV version of this room (Locus 203; fig.
16) was abandoned shortly after it was built, and mudbrick rubble filled
the room. Subsequently its southwestern end was cut by a large pit from
Level III.

Surprisingly few small finds were recovered from this building.
There were several reasons for this. The floors of the upper two levels
had been badly cut up; very little archaeological material from them
remained to be examined. Level IV, for example, was represented only by
parts of two rooms, Loci 208 and 211. Secondly, the burials, which
often contained burial gifts in this period, had already been excavated
by the Pennsylvania expedition. Finally, abandoned objects were gener—
ally not found on the floors here, unlike in Area WC-2.

At the end of its life, this house was not replaced by another
building. The next level, III, contained no architectural features, but
included several pits which cut down into the house. Several of the
pottery types from Level III were not found in Levels VI-IV. Level II
was represented by more than two meters of sloping layers of ashy debris
containing Seleucid and Achaemenid sherds, but no architectural remains.
This area was apparently a refuse dump at that time. Level I, at the
surface of the tell, included only wall foundations for now-vanished
buildings.

It can be seen that the sixteenth season's work did not entirely

achieve its principal aims, which were to elucidate the ceramic sequence

52

of the post-Kassite period and place the finds from Area WC in a larger
stratigraphical context. The lower limit for the Area WC-2 corpus of
ceramic types must be constructed from the relatively limited numbers of
sherds collected from TA IV and III. The upper limit was entirely
lacking; from the evidence of the pottery, there seemed to be an occupa-
tional hiatus in Area TC, just as there was in Area WC, during the early
post-Kassite centuries.

As was mentioned previously, the ceramic types found in Levels VI-
IV in Area TC were also found in Area WC-2. However there were dif-
ferences in the relative frequencies of types among the levels of the
two areas. These differences and their chronological implications will
be examined in the following chapter.

The results from the excavations in Area TC have made necessary a
thorough reevaluation of the late-second and early first-millennium
levels in the neighboring Area TA. When excavation levels were matched
across the meter-wide baulk which separated the two areas, it was disco-
vered that, on the basis of both wall alignments and absolute eleva—
tions, TC IV matched up with TA IV and V (figs. 22 and 23). This,
however, created a problem: TA V was the earliest first-millennium
level on the north side of the baulk, while to the south in Area TC two
earlier versions of the first-millennium house remained to be accounted
for. The walls of the first of these, TC V, seemed to disappear inside
the baulk, because in TA VI there was only an outside space dated to the
Kassite period (fig. 21). The mystery deepened when TC VI and TA VIL

were compared (fig. 20): while the walls on either side of the baulk

53
lined up properly, and they indisputably belonged to the same house, the
TC walls were certainly from the early first millennium while the TA
walls were published as Kassite. Clearly there were serious stratigra-
phical problems in Area TA involving the Kassite and later levels.
These problems, their solution, and a proposal for the rehabilitation of
the Area TA material form the basis of part II (chapters 3-5) of this
study. Before these questions can be explored, however, a ceramic se-
quence must be constructed for late second- and early first-millennium

Nippur; and it is to this task we now turn.

Typology

In the Introduction to this study, the lack of a pottery sequence

Kassite kingdom. In this chapter, an attempt at the construction of

The levels in Area TA were distinguished from one another by
changes in the plans of the buildings through time; such differences
included anything from the reconstruction of a building with minor
alterations in plan to the outright replacement of one building by
another. In an area as large as TA, the task of identifying an
architectural level across the entire excavation involves correlating
the internal levels among several different buildings, each of which has
its own constructional history; usually this process takes place after
the field season is over, and it is not always neat. Particularly in
domestic areas like TA, buildings can differ in the time, frequency, and
thoroughness of their renovations. In the absence of thorough-going de-
structions or abandonments, archaeologists may have to approximate the
beginning and end of an architectural level, recognizing that the
"level" is in fact part of a continuum.20

In Area TA, however, these potential difficulties were not ad—
dressed. Each level was defined while it was being dug. The general
procedure was to identify the bottom of a level by digging down in a
room until an architectural change was observed. That change was then
traced throughout the building by following the floor at which it oc-
curred. Floors were not traced between buildings. Usually, though,
architectural changes could be found at approximately the same absolute
elevation in all the buildings of the area. By assuming that these
alterations were contemporary with one another because they were at the

Conclusions

When the first-millennium city expanded to reoccupy Tablet Hill, a
pattern of cadastral boundaries was established that lasted through
several subsequent architectural renovations. This can be seen clearly
at the southern end where the public thoroughfares remained unchanged
despite apparent shifts in property lines among the surrounding houses.

Those shifts are most apparent at the northern end of the area.
With House 107 and the Kassite street removed from the first-millennium
plans, the case for a second cadastral survey here, as suggested in OIP
78,18 is considerably weakened. This northern area appears instead to
have been an open space or yard into which surrounding houses might
expand or otherwise compete for space. For example, a passageway ini-'
tially separated House C from TA 70 in Level V*. Subsequently, however,
House C was enlarged right up to the other house's back wall. The con-
struction of House B entailed an adjustment in the northwest boundary of
House 76 and a reorientation of the latter house as well.

The fixed property lines at the southern end of Area TA suggest
that during this period Tablet Hill was criss-crossed by a permanent

network of streets that ran parallel and perpendicular to the mid-city

represented the middle of a block of houses defined by the street

Occupational density, as measured by the size and number of houses,
reached a peak during the latter part of the seventh century, represen—
ted in Area TA by Level ILI* Early. Thereafter the density of the
settled area slowly decreased as houses were abandoned and never re-
built. The beginning of this trend can be seen in Level III* with the
sequential abandonment of Houses C and TC. The process continued in
Level II* and later with the abandonment of Houses 76 and 41. Finally,
only House B remained, sharing the area with two thin walls, seen on the
plan of TA II, running parallel to each other about 20 meters apart;
these are apparently the remains of an animal pen or, perhaps, a garden.

As the number of houses decreased, their quality increased. The
generally thinner walls and irregularities of plan that characterized
the houses of the eighth and seventh centuries tended to disappear
through time. The solid, rectilinear walls of House B (Level III*)
clearly stood apart from the likes of Houses C and TC with their rounded
corners and House 76 with its projecting vestibule. House 76's own
renovation in Level III* resulted in another thick-walled rectilinear
house. House B's painted walls in Level III* have already been men-
tioned; in Level II* this substantial house was made even larger. House

Figure 60 shows the proposed correlation of levels between Areas

frequencies (tables 5, 7, and 8), which show that the WC-2 levels are
approximately contemporary with TC Levels V and IV (=TA Levels IV* and

New types, which are associated chronologically with the period of
Achaemenid rule, appear in TA II*. The pottery evidence for TA II* is
confirmed by the presence of tablets dated to early Achaemenid rulers in
that level.

rather than sooner after the middle of the seventh century. Moreover,
as was suggested in chapter 2, the presence of Assyrian-related pottery
types is chronologically inconclusive in the context of the relatively
short stratigraphic sequence of Area WC-2. However, in the course of
the longer sequence of Area TA, vessels with Assyrian affinities appear
for the first (and only) time at the beginning of Level III*, As was
argued in chapter 4, it is reasonable to regard the first appearance of
these vessels as a manifestation of the close association between the
Assyrians and Nippur in the latter half of the seventh century. There—
fore, given the general similarity of the pottery between the WC-2 lev-
els and TA IV* and III*, it is possible to attribute WC-2 II to the last
decades of Assyrian rule. WC-2 I, then, should extend into the sixth

century, through at least the first part of the Neo-Babylonian empire.

especially Babylon and Ur.!04 The inference is that these Assyrian-type

coffins were first used by wealthier members of the community; only

The events of the last quarter of the seventh century are not iden-
tifiable in the remains elsewhere on the site. The population of Tablet
Hill, as measured by the number of occupied houses in Area TA, may have
begun to decline at about this time; but the prosperity of the area
seems, if anything, to have been on the increase. From the archaeologi-
cal evidence, we may conclude that after a period of turmoil, the city
adapted successfully to life under the new regime.

Thereafter, the city presented a much lower profile on Babylonia's
religious and political landscape. Nippur is infrequently mentioned in
the royal inscriptions of the Neo-Babylonian kings,!! and royally spon-
sored work on its major temples seems to have been of modest
proportions. The only known construction associated with a Neo-
Babylonian king is Nebuchadnezzar II's repair work in the Ekur.!12
There is nothing at Nippur to be compared to the massive building pro—
jects that were undertaken at other cities. Essentially unchanged,
Esarhaddon's and Ashurbanipal's temples continued to serve the needs of

their constituencies for many decades, if not centuries. Perhaps this

royal neglect of the city and its institutions was punishment because
the city had initially resisted Nabopolassar. It should also be remem-
bered that seventh-century Nippur played a special, if poorly
understood, role in the Assyrian imperial administration. The loss of
that role would assuredly have resulted in a diminution of the city's
vitality. For whatever reasons, the transfer of allegiance from Nineveh
to Babylon was, for Nippur, the end of an era.

As this study has shown, Nippur's archaeology and history from the
thirteenth to the sixth centuries mirror in many respects that of
Babylonia as a whole. The city and the state each experienced a serious
decline during the final decades of Kassite rule. For both, the darkest
years were those of the tenth century; and in each case the recovery
that began in the eighth century was sustained through the period of
Assyrian domination and culminated in the establishment of the Neo-
Babylonian empire. !13

There were, however, significant differences. Nippur's decline in
the 1220s, apparently due to a loss of its water supply, was catas—
trophic, resulting in the outright abandonment of much of the city.
Until this disaster, Nippur was at the center of the Kassite kingdom,
not only geographically, but economically and religiously; and it ap-
pears to have benefited greatly from royal patronage. To some degree,
Nippur's continued geographic centrality may have been artificial: the

settlement maps suggest that the long-term westward shift of the

Euphrates was already in process and that much of the eastern, central,
and southern alluvium continued to be bound hydrologically to the west
only through the construction and maintenance of large canais. 114

In any event, by the end of the twelfth century, Nippur and its
affairs were clearly peripheral. The city was now on the southeastern
edge of the urban heartland; its economy was functioning only at a low
level and was probably only of local significance; and Enlil, the chief
god of the city and of the nation, had been deposed by Marduk of
Babylon. !15

From the dearth of documentary and archaeological evidence, one
gets the impression that the settlement at Nippur dropped below the
threshold of urbanism during the course of the following centuries. At
times it may have consisted of little more than a village huddled in the
shadow of the ziggurat. We do not know the degree to which this may
have been true of other Babylonian cities. The documentary evidence is
similarly sparse elsewhere. However, since virtually nothing is known
about the presence or absence of archaeological levels of this time
range at other sites, except for Babylon and Isin, it is impossible to
make comparisons with the negative evidence from Nippur.

Finally, Nippur's great expansion in the seventh century may have
been due to the special circumstances surrounding its position as an
Assyrian center. Under the patronage of their Assyrian overlords, the

city and its temples blossomed for one last time.

In the reconstruction offered here, particular attention has been
paid to the potential role the environment played in shaping Nippur's
destiny. Nevertheless, it cannot yet be conclusively demonstrated that
the Euphrates abandoned its Nippur channel during the decade of the
1220s. Though compelling, the evidence lacks the requisite chronolo-
gical and geographical specificity. The case for severe drought in the
eleventh and tenth centuries thus far is also circumstantial. In any
event, the story of Nippur after the Kassites vividly illustrates the
fragility of urban life in the environment of the alluvial plain. As
historians, anthropologists, and archaeologists approach questions of
causation from their various points of view, they must not fail to con-
sider environmental factors, particularly as more recent specialist
studies display increasing methodological sophistication in handling
complex data, 116

There are ample opportunities for further research over the whole

range of topics treated in this study. As regards Nippur itself, it
would be desirable to find and excavate levels belonging to the set~
tlement that existed here between the twelfth and eighth centuries.
This may prove, however, to be an impossible task. Besides the expense
involved in moving the dumps around the ziggurat, an additional negative
consideration is the likelihood that the Parthian builders removed much
of the putative settlement during the course of their massive building

operations.

Given the situation at Nippur, a more feasible project would be the
further horizontal exposure of the seventh-century levels at Area WC-2.
These levels lie just below the modern surface and offer a ready oppor—
tunity for the synchronic investigation of a residential quarter that
flourished and declined over a period of only several decades.

For Babylonia as a whole, the most urgent archaeological task is
still the description and chronological ordering of the ceramics. The
thirteenth-century materials seem to be in good order at Nippur, as are
those from the eighth and seventh centuries. It remains to be shown,
however, the extent to which the Nippur corpus is typical for Babylonia
as a whole; there are bound to be regional variations that must be taken
into account.1!7 The remainder of the period is essentially unknown,
despite the preliminary steps undertaken here to define distinctive
shapes of the post-Kassite assemblage. All the available evidence sug-
gests that the pottery sequence is to be found in the urban centers of
the western alluvium (for example, Babylon, Borsippa, and Dilbat).
Ironically, even though most of the written evidence for this period
derives from these cities, to date we know virtually nothing about their
archaeological remains. At this stage of our knowledge, even a limited
exposure of the relevant levels in one of these sites would represent a

step forward. With an increased knowledge of the ceramic indicators, we

could more confidently identify late second- and early first-millennium

The archaeological material from Nippur has permitted us to create
at least an outline of the site's occupational history during a poorly-
documented period. We have seen also some of the questions we must ask
if we are to understand the complex political, social, and environmental
interactions that characterized Babylonia in the centuries after the
Kassites. Nippur, however, was on the periphery of Babylonian state
control during this span of time and was at times, perhaps, even beyond
the pale. The best, most complete answers to our questions concerning
the archaeology and history of Babylonia in the late second and early
first millennia will, therefore, not be found at Nippur. We must focus
our archaeological attention on the heartland of that state if we are to

shed more light on these dark centuries.
